content_html:
Brain ⇄ Mind Dynamic in Evolution

Evolution has not “stopped” biologically, but the main arena of rapid change has shifted upward to the level of mind and culture. Genes select potentials; brains change via plasticity; minds reconstruct models; culture scales reconstruction through institutions and technology; feedback loops alter selection.

Classical Biological Evolution operates through variation, selection, inheritance in genes. It operates over millions of years, DNA and physiology lead to brains, bodies, perceptual systems. Once brains reached a certain critical complexity, cultural and mental processes started evolving faster than genes. Neural plasticity allows individuals to change within a lifetime (learning, memory), and cultural transmission (stories, art, rituals) enables non-genetic inheritance. Memes and ideas evolve through minds — variation (reinterpretation), selection (what spreads), inheritance (teaching/recording).

The biological and mental levels are nested: genes build brains, brains support minds, minds create culture, which feeds back to reshape environments, which influences which genes thrive (gene–culture coevolution). Today, many evolutionary pressures act primarily through brain/mind/culture; technology & knowledge systems evolve on the scale of years, not millennia. Distributed cognition (societies, networks, AI) acts as a new evolutionary substrate. Biological evolution still continues — but at human timescales, mind-based dynamics dominate.

You could think of evolution as a layered system:

  • Genes (slow code)
  • Brains (medium, plastic code)
  • Minds & culture (fast, distributed code)

Each layer still evolves, but the dominant signal of adaptation now flows through the brain/mind/cultural layer. Evolution now manifests less in genetic change and more in brain/mind dynamics — learning, memory, culture, and distributed systems. But it’s not a replacement: it’s a stacked system, where faster-evolving cultural/mental processes sit atop slower biological ones.

Stacked Evolution

Genes → Brains → Minds → Culture/Distributed Cognition

Biological evolution remains foundational, but rapid evolutionary dynamics now manifest through brains, minds, and distributed culture — with feedback loops (gene–culture coevolution, niche construction).

Genes (Slow Code)

  • Mechanism: Variation → Selection → Inheritance (DNA).
  • Timescale: 10^3–10^6 years (context-dependent; can be faster under strong selection).
  • Products: Neuroanatomy, metabolism, sensory systems.
  • Example: Lactase persistence emerging with dairying cultures (gene–culture coevolution).

Brains (Plastic Hardware)

  • Mechanism: Neural plasticity; learning-dependent wiring; memory consolidation/reconsolidation.
  • Timescale: Seconds → decades (lifespan).
  • Products: Perception, skill, habit; biases (agency detection, ToM).
  • Example: Literacy reshapes cortical networks (cultural practice → neural reorganisation).

Minds (Fast Models)

  • Mechanism: Inference, simulation, memory reconstruction; social learning.
  • Timescale: Milliseconds → years.
  • Products: Ideas, beliefs, goals; spiritual frames; innovations.
  • Example: Norms that spread via prestige/imitative learning.

Culture & Distributed Cognition (Networked Code)

  • Mechanism: Social transmission, institutions, writing, computation, AI; selection on ideas (“memes”).
  • Timescale: Days → centuries (much faster than genes).
  • Products: Technologies, laws, religions, science; external memory (archives, code, media).
  • Example: Dairying practices → selection for lactase persistence; digital infrastructures reshaping attention.

Key Claims

  • Dual inheritance: Humans inherit both genes and culture; both evolve with partly distinct mechanisms.
  • Speed shift: Cultural evolution typically operates orders of magnitude faster than genetic evolution.
  • Feedback: Cultural practices alter selection pressures (e.g., dairying → lactase genes).
  • Distributed mind: Cognition extends across tools, institutions, and networks.
  • Transmission Media Genes: DNA replication, reproduction.
  • Brains: Hebbian learning, synaptic plasticity.
  • Minds: Imitation, instruction, inference.
  • Culture: Language, writing, schooling, platforms, code.

All levels interact continuously; no level “replaces” another.
